ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: The upper part of the figure is 甲, the vertical axis is labeled i/A, and the horizontal axis is t/(×10^-2 s). The dashed lines mark the current peak values +1 A and -1 A. The waveform of 甲 is a sinusoidal pulse: in the intervals 0～2, 4～6, 6～8, 10～12, etc., half of a sinusoidal pulse appears, with peak magnitude 1 A; among them, 0～2 is a positive half-wave, 4～6 is a negative half-wave, and in the intervals 2～4 and 8～10, etc., the current is 0. From the figure, the period of 甲 can be taken as 6×10^-2 s; within one period it contains two half-sinusoidal segments each lasting 2×10^-2 s and one zero-current segment lasting 2×10^-2 s. The lower part is 乙, the vertical axis is likewise labeled i/A, and the horizontal axis is t/(×10^-2 s). The square wave only jumps between +1 A and -1 A; there is no zero-current platform in the figure, so the magnitude of the current at any moment is 1 A. Then reason: The electric work consumed in the same resistor R is W=∫i^2Rdt. The two resistors are completely identical, and the energizing time is both 1 min, so to compare W it is only necessary to compare the time average value of the square of the current. For 甲, within one period T=6×10^-2 s, each half-sinusoidal segment lasts 2×10^-2 s, and the peak value is 1 A. The average value of sin^2 within a half-sinusoidal segment is 1/2, so the contribution of one half-sinusoidal segment to ∫i^2dt is (2×10^-2)×(1^2/2). Within one period there are two such nonzero half-sinusoidal segments, therefore ∫i^2dt=2×[(2×10^-2)×(1^2/2)]=2×10^-2. Dividing by the period 6×10^-2 gives the average i^2 of 甲 as 1/3. 乙 always satisfies |i|=1 A, so the average i^2=1. Therefore W_甲:W_乙=(1/3):1=1:3.
